title: 19. Dynamic Programming Fundamentals
description: Master Dynamic Programming in Java: Overlapping subproblems, optimal substructure, top-down memoization, bottom-up tabulation, state transitions, space optimization, 1D linear DP (Fibonacci, Climbing Stairs, Min Cost Stairs, House Robber I & II), Knapsack DP (0/1 Knapsack, Unbounded Knapsack, Subset Sum, Partition Equal Subset), Coin Change I & II, String & Subsequence DP (LCS, LIS, Edit Distance), and Interval DP (Matrix Chain Multiplication).
topics: Dynamic Programming Philosophy: Avoiding redundant recomputations through subproblem caching and bottom-up building
Overlapping Subproblems: Recursion tree analysis, repeated evaluation detection, and call tree memoization
Optimal Substructure: Building globally optimal solutions from optimal subproblem answers
Top-Down Memoization: Caching recursive results with arrays/HashMaps, pruning recursive branches, and stack depth limits
Bottom-Up Tabulation: Iterative state propagation from base cases to target state without call stack overhead
6-Step Conversion Recipe: Naive recursion -> identify state -> memoization -> loop conversion -> tabulation -> space reduction
DP State Formulation: Defining parameters (1D index, 2D capacity/indices, 3D constraints) capturing all required decision history
State Transitions & Recurrences: Formulating decision logic (include vs exclude, pick min/max, sum independent ways)
Base Cases & Boundary Anchors: Correct initialization values, sentinel flags (-1 vs 0), and handling unreachable states (INF)
Space Optimization: Sliding pointer variables O(1), 2-row rolling buffers, and in-place 1D backward array sweeps
1D Linear DP: Fibonacci quad-strategy comparison, Climbing Stairs, Min Cost Stairs, and House Robber I & II
0/1 Knapsack DP: Include/exclude paradigm, 2D matrix dry runs, and reverse 1D array traversal
Unbounded Knapsack: Forward capacity propagation with infinite item supply, comparison with 0/1 Knapsack
Subset Sum & Partition Equal Subset: Boolean DP matrices, reduction of array partition to target totalSum / 2
Coin Change I & II: Fewest coins minimization vs total combinations counting with coin outer loop order
Longest Common Subsequence (LCS): 2D character matching, DP matrix construction, and backtracking string reconstruction
Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS): O(N²) standard DP vs O(N log N) patience sorting with Arrays.binarySearch
Edit Distance (Levenshtein): Insert, delete, and replace transitions on 2D string grid with alignment recovery
Interval DP (Matrix Chain Multiplication): Iterating over chain length L, split points k, and optimal parenthesization
Comprehensive Practice & Checklist: 35 LeetCode/FAANG problems across 4 levels and 20-point mastery diagnostic

scenarios.title: Cloud Resource Capacity & Workload Knapsack Allocation
scenarios.description: A cloud orchestrator must schedule batch jobs onto bare-metal compute instances with fixed RAM capacity to maximize throughput value where each job can either run completely or be queued.
scenarios.solution: Model the problem as a 0/1 Knapsack where instance RAM is capacity W, job memory demands are weights wt, and job revenue yields are values val. Execute bottom-up 1D reverse-swept DP in O(N * W) time and O(W) auxiliary space.

scenarios.title: Autonomous Drone Battery-Constrained Flight Pathing
scenarios.description: An aerial drone must navigate a stepped waypoint climb where jumping 1 or 2 altitude gates expends varying kilowatt-hours, requiring the minimum battery depletion route to high altitude.
scenarios.solution: Apply the Minimum Cost Climbing Stairs dynamic programming formulation: dp[i] = cost[i] + Math.min(dp[i-1], dp[i-2]). Maintain two rolling scalar variables (prev1, prev2) for O(1) auxiliary memory on the microcontroller.

scenarios.title: Automated DNA Genomic Sequence Alignment
scenarios.description: A bioinformatics pipeline needs to compare two mutated viral genome sequences and identify the minimum number of single-nucleotide insertions, deletions, and substitutions to align them.
scenarios.solution: Execute Edit Distance (Levenshtein Distance) DP in O(M * N) time using a 2D table dp[i][j]. If nucleotide characters match, take diagonal dp[i-1][j-1]; otherwise, evaluate 1 + Math.min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j-1]). Backtrack pointers to reconstruct the exact mutation alignment.

questions.question: What are the two foundational properties a problem must possess to be effectively solved by Dynamic Programming?
options: Overlapping Subproblems and Optimal Substructure.
Greedy Choice Property and Independence of States.
Logarithmic Tree Height and Bounded Degree.
Continuous Variables and Convex Differentiability.
questions.explanation: Dynamic Programming requires Overlapping Subproblems (the same subproblems are solved repeatedly) and Optimal Substructure (the globally optimal solution can be constructed from optimal solutions to its subproblems).

questions.question: What is the primary operational difference between Top-Down Memoization and Bottom-Up Tabulation in Java?
options: Memoization is recursive and computes only required states on demand but risks StackOverflowError on deep recursions; Tabulation is iterative and computes all table states systematically from base cases using loops.
Memoization always runs in O(N²) time while Tabulation runs in O(N) time.
Memoization does not use auxiliary memory, whereas Tabulation requires disk storage.
Tabulation cannot solve optimization problems.
questions.explanation: Top-Down DP starts from the target state and recursively caches subproblem solutions as needed (on-demand), risking JVM call stack overflow for large N. Bottom-Up DP starts from base cases and fills the DP table iteratively using loops, with zero recursion overhead.

questions.question: When converting naive recursive Fibonacci fib(n) to Dynamic Programming, how does the time complexity transform?
options: From exponential O(2ⁿ) to linear O(n).
From O(n!) to O(n²).
From O(n²) to O(log n).
From O(n log n) to O(1).
questions.explanation: Naive recursive Fibonacci forms a binary tree of height n with 2ⁿ calls due to massive duplicate recomputation. DP computes each of the n distinct subproblems exactly once in O(1) time each, reducing time complexity to O(n).

questions.question: In the Climbing Stairs problem where a climber can take 1 or 2 steps, why is the recurrence relation dp[i] = dp[i - 1] + dp[i - 2]?
options: To land on step i, the final step must have originated either from step i-1 (via a 1-step jump) or from step i-2 (via a 2-step jump). By the addition principle of counting, total ways is the sum of ways to both previous steps.
Because stairs always follow an arithmetic progression.
Because taking 2 steps doubles the previous number of combinations.
Because step i requires computing the square root of the step count.
questions.explanation: Any valid sequence of steps reaching step i must end with either a 1-step leap (originating from step i-1) or a 2-step leap (originating from step i-2). Since these two final actions are mutually exclusive, the total distinct ways is dp[i-1] + dp[i-2].

questions.question: In the Minimum Cost Climbing Stairs problem, what does the recurrence dp[i] = cost[i] + Math.min(dp[i - 1], dp[i - 2]) represent?
options: The minimum cumulative cost to step onto step i, paying its fee and coming from the cheaper of the previous two steps.
The total sum of all stairs visited up to step i.
The average cost per step climbed.
The maximum cost allowed before the climber terminates.
questions.explanation: To occupy step i, you must pay cost[i] plus the minimum accumulated cost to reach step i, which could only have been entered from step i-1 or step i-2.

questions.question: Why does a greedy approach fail on the House Robber problem (e.g., [2, 7, 9, 3, 1] or [100, 1, 1, 100])?
options: A local greedy choice to rob a high-value house locks out both its neighbors, which could have yielded a greater combined sum than the single house.
Greedy algorithms cannot compare integers in Java.
Greedy sorting modifies the original house addresses.
Greedy choices always result in negative sums.
questions.explanation: In [100, 1, 1, 100] or [2, 10, 10, 2], greedy picking may take a locally tempting value but prevents robbing multiple adjacent neighbors that produce a superior global loot total. DP evaluates both include (nums[i] + dp[i-2]) and exclude (dp[i-1]).

questions.question: In House Robber II where houses are arranged in a circular ring (house 0 is adjacent to house n-1), how is the circular constraint solved with standard DP?
options: By running the linear House Robber algorithm twice: once for houses 0 to n-2 (excluding the last house), and once for houses 1 to n-1 (excluding the first house), returning Math.max of both.
By duplicating the entire array and running Kadane's algorithm.
By sorting the houses in descending order of cash.
By applying Dijkstra's algorithm along the perimeter.
questions.explanation: Because house 0 and house n-1 cannot both be robbed simultaneously, at least one of them must be left unrobbed. This cleanly breaks the circle into two standard linear problems: subarray [0 ... n-2] and subarray [1 ... n-1].

questions.question: In the standard 2D 0/1 Knapsack DP table dp[i][w], what does cell dp[i][w] represent?
options: The maximum value obtainable using a subset of the first i items with a maximum weight capacity of w.
The minimum weight required to pack i items.
The index of the heaviest item included in capacity w.
The total number of ways to pack exactly i items.
questions.explanation: The DP state dp[i][w] represents the maximum profit/value achievable by considering the first i items under a total weight limit of w.

questions.question: When compressing the 0/1 Knapsack table to a 1D array dp[w], why MUST the capacity loop iterate in reverse from W down to wt[i]?
options: Iterating backwards ensures that dp[w - wt[i]] represents the value from the previous item tier (i - 1), preventing the current item i from being included multiple times.
Iterating forward causes ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException in Java.
Iterating backwards sorts the items by value density.
Backward iteration is required by the JVM JIT compiler.
questions.explanation: If we iterate forward (from wt[i] to W), an updated value in dp[w - wt[i]] would represent item i having already been included, allowing item i to be included repeatedly (which turns it into Unbounded Knapsack). Backward iteration preserves the single-use invariant of 0/1 Knapsack.

questions.question: Why does Unbounded Knapsack intentionally iterate capacity w forward from wt[i] up to W?
options: Because each item has unlimited copies, so updating dp[w] from a previously updated dp[w - wt[i]] in the current pass allows multiple instances of item i to be chosen.
Because backward iteration in unbounded knapsack creates integer underflow.
Because unbounded knapsack cannot be solved using 2D DP.
Because items in unbounded knapsack must have negative weights.
questions.explanation: In Unbounded Knapsack, an item can be chosen infinitely many times. Forward iteration allows dp[w] to build directly on top of dp[w - wt[i]] that already contains one or more instances of the same item i.

questions.question: In the Subset Sum Problem, what does boolean dp[i][j] represent?
options: Whether a subset of the first i elements can sum to exactly j.
The number of elements required to sum to j.
The maximum element used in a subset summing to j.
Whether element i is greater than target j.
questions.explanation: In Subset Sum, dp[i][j] is a boolean flag indicating if there is any subset chosen from the first i numbers whose elements sum exactly to target j.

questions.question: How can the Partition Equal Subset Sum problem be reduced to the Subset Sum problem?
options: If totalSum is odd, equal partition is impossible (return false); otherwise, search for a subset summing to totalSum / 2.
Sort the array and check if the median equals the mean.
Divide the array into odd and even numbers and check if both lengths match.
Sum the array and take modulo 3.
questions.explanation: Partitioning into two subsets of equal sum requires each subset to sum to totalSum / 2. If totalSum is odd, integer division by 2 is impossible. If even, the problem is identical to finding a subset summing to target = totalSum / 2.

questions.question: In Coin Change I (finding minimum coins to make amount A), what base initialization is used for dp array of size A + 1?
options: dp[0] = 0, and all other dp[i] initialized to amount + 1 (or INF) to indicate unreachable amounts.
All elements initialized to 0.
All elements initialized to -1.
All elements initialized to Integer.MAX_VALUE without checking overflow.
questions.explanation: Since we seek the minimum, unreachable amounts are initialized to a sentinel larger than any possible answer (like amount + 1), and dp[0] = 0 because 0 coins are needed to produce amount 0.

questions.question: In Coin Change II (number of unique combinations to make amount A), why must the outer loop iterate over coins and the inner loop over amounts?
options: Iterating coins in the outer loop enforces that coins are considered in a fixed order, counting unique combinations rather than ordered permutations (order does not matter).
Iterating amounts outer would cause an OutOfMemoryError.
Because Java arrays only permit coin iteration first.
To ensure all coins are sorted in descending order.
questions.explanation: If amounts are in the outer loop, {1, 2} and {2, 1} would both be counted as distinct paths (permutations). Putting coins in the outer loop ensures coin 2 is never placed before coin 1 in any combination, ensuring only unique combinations are counted.

questions.question: In Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) between strings s1 and s2, if s1.charAt(i - 1) == s2.charAt(j - 1), what is the state transition?
options: dp[i][j] = Math.max(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1]);
questions.explanation: When the current characters match, they extend the longest common subsequence formed by the prefixes of s1 and s2 up to indices i-1 and j-1 by exactly 1 character: 1 + dp[i-1][j-1].

questions.question: How does the Patience Sorting / Binary Search algorithm solve Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS) in O(N log N) time?
options: It maintains an array 'tails' of smallest tail elements of all increasing subsequences found so far, updating or extending via binary search (Arrays.binarySearch).
It builds a binary search tree of all prefixes.
It sorts the array in O(N log N) and takes the longest run.
It executes Dijkstra's algorithm across numerical differences.
questions.explanation: By maintaining `tails[i]`, which stores the smallest tail of all increasing subsequences of length i + 1, each incoming element can either replace an existing tail or extend the maximum length using binary search in O(log N) time per element.

questions.question: In Edit Distance (Levenshtein Distance) between word1 and word2, if characters mismatch at indices i and j, which three operations are minimized?
options: 1 + Math.min(dp[i - 1][j] /* delete */, Math.min(dp[i][j - 1] /* insert */, dp[i - 1][j - 1] /* replace */));
Math.min(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1]) - 1;
1 + Math.max(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1]);
questions.explanation: A mismatch can be resolved by deleting character i from word1 (state dp[i-1][j]), inserting character j into word1 (state dp[i][j-1]), or replacing character i with character j (state dp[i-1][j-1]). Each operation carries a cost of 1.

questions.question: In Matrix Chain Multiplication, why is it categorized as Interval DP?
options: Because subproblems are defined over index intervals [i, j] representing matrix chains, and the DP table is filled in increasing order of interval chain length L = j - i + 1.
Because matrices can only be multiplied over time intervals.
Because it operates on intervals of continuous floating-point numbers.
Because matrix dimensions must form closed mathematical intervals.
questions.explanation: Interval DP defines subproblems on sub-ranges [i, j] of an array. To solve for range [i, j], all smaller sub-intervals [i, k] and [k+1, j] must already be solved, requiring loops structured by interval length L.

questions.question: What is a dangerous bug when initializing a memoization array in Java with default 0 when valid subproblem solutions can be 0?
options: The algorithm cannot distinguish between an uncomputed subproblem and a subproblem whose solved optimal value is 0, causing redundant recomputations and degrading to exponential time.
Java throws an ArrayStoreException.
The JVM garbage collects the array automatically.
The returned answer is multiplied by 0.
questions.explanation: If a subproblem legitimately evaluates to 0 (such as 0 ways or 0 cost), checking `if (memo[state] != 0)` fails to detect that it was already computed, re-executing the recursive call tree every time and destroying the DP caching benefit.

questions.question: When is space optimization (e.g., reducing 2D DP to 1D or O(1) rolling variables) NOT possible or inadvisable?
options: When the problem requires reconstructing the actual optimal sequence of choices (reconstructing the LCS string, which items to pack, or the path taken) rather than just the numeric optimal value.
When the array length exceeds 10,000.
When elements are negative.
When using Java 17 or higher.
questions.explanation: To backtrack and reconstruct the exact items chosen, path taken, or LCS characters, you need the complete matrix of transitions. Overwriting previous rows or states destroys the pointer trail necessary for path reconstruction.
